young.html: In 1831 a young Frenchman named Alexis de Tocqueville (say TOKE-vil) sailed to the United States with his best friend, Gustave de Beaumont. They were supposed to study prisons. But Tocqueville wanted to understand something much bigger: how a whole country could govern itself without a king.

For nine months they traveled by stagecoach, horseback and steamboat, from New England to the frontier forests, down the Mississippi to New Orleans, and back to Washington. They talked to farmers, lawyers, pioneers and the president. Then Tocqueville went home and wrote a famous book about what he saw.

young.html: What surprised him most? Americans were more equal than the people of Europe, and they loved to join together to get things done: to build a school, start a library or help neighbors, without waiting for the government to do it.

Be Tocqueville. Imagine a visitor from another country spending a week in your town. Write a short letter home as that visitor: what three things would surprise them most? What would they admire, and what might worry them?

full.html: Alexis de Tocqueville (1805–1859) came from an old French noble family; several relatives had died in the Terror of the French Revolution. A young magistrate, he sailed with Gustave de Beaumont in 1831 on an official mission to study American prisons. They landed at Newport in May 1831 and left New York in February 1832. Volume 1 of Democracy in America came out in 1835, Volume 2 in 1840, both translated into English by Henry Reeve. Tocqueville later served in the French parliament and, briefly in 1849, as foreign minister.

full.text: Amongst the novel objects that attracted my attention during my stay in the United States, nothing struck me more forcibly than the general equality of conditions. I readily discovered the prodigious influence which this primary fact exercises on the whole course of society ...
full.author: Tocqueville
full.note: Reeve's translation first appeared in 1835 and 1840.

full.html: Tocqueville thought equality was the great fact of the modern world, coming to Europe too, whether Europeans liked it or not. He wrote to help his countrymen see both its blessings and its dangers, so they could keep liberty alive within it.

items: Local self-government. In the New England township, citizens run their own affairs. Tocqueville thought this is where Americans learn to be free.
Federalism and the Constitution, which he studied closely, along with The Federalist.
Courts and juries, which teach ordinary people the habits of law.
A free press, many newspapers rather than a few.
Religion, separate from the state, which he thought shaped American habits of self-restraint.

full.text: Americans of all ages, all conditions, and all dispositions, constantly form associations. They have not only commercial and manufacturing companies, in which all take part, but associations of a thousand other kinds—religious, moral, serious, futile, extensive, or restricted, enormous or diminutive.
full.author: Tocqueville
full.work: Democracy in America, Volume 2, Part II, Chapter V

full.html: Tocqueville admired America, but he was not a cheerleader. He warned of the tyranny of the majority, not mainly through unjust laws but through the pressure of opinion: "I know no country in which there is so little true independence of mind and freedom of discussion as in America," he wrote, in Reeve's words. He worried that individualism would lead people to retreat into private life and leave public affairs to others, and that a gentle, all-providing government, a soft despotism, could keep citizens in a kind of permanent childhood.

He wrote at length about the three races of America. He judged slavery a great evil that degraded the society that practiced it, foresaw grave conflict over it, and described the forced removal of Native American nations with sorrow, having watched Choctaw families cross the icy Mississippi at Memphis.
Tocqueville's method was to look beneath laws at habits of the heart: the customs, beliefs and daily practices that make a free government work or fail.
Reading Tocqueville as simply praising or simply criticizing America. He set out the strengths and the dangers side by side, and readers of every political leaning have found support in him.

items: Montesquieu, whom Tocqueville read constantly, taught him to study how laws fit a people's customs and circumstances.
The Federalist (earlier on this ladder; see the American History & Civics Ladder's Federalist Papers) gave him the American founders' own account of their Constitution.
Mill, next to him in this era, reviewed both volumes and took from them the fear of the tyranny of the majority.
Tocqueville's later book, The Old Regime and the Revolution (1856), asked why France's revolution ended in centralized power.

questions: What groups or clubs does your family belong to? What do they do that the government does not?
Tocqueville worried people might go along with the crowd. Have you ever been afraid to disagree with a group?
What would a visitor from far away notice first about your town?
Why do you think Tocqueville thought local government was a school of freedom?
Tocqueville saw both good and bad in America. Why is it important to see both in something you love?
